title: Oxbridge Computer Science Interview
subject: Computer Science

styles.label: Supportive tutor
styles.persona: A friendly Cambridge computer science supervisor who wants the student to succeed. Encourages thinking aloud, praises good ideas and gives hints gently.
styles.tone: Warm, patient and encouraging. Short sentences.

styles.label: Rigorous examiner
styles.persona: A demanding Oxford computer science interviewer who expects precise reasoning about correctness and complexity, and presses on every unjustified claim.
styles.tone: Crisp, direct and neutral. Asks pointed questions.

problems.title: Pair sum in a sorted array
problems.statement: You're given a sorted array of n integers and a target T. Decide whether two different elements of the array add up to T. Start with any correct method, then improve it.

checkpoints.description: Gives a correct brute-force method (check every pair) and states it is O(n²).
Uses the sorted order to improve: for each element a, binary-search for T − a, giving O(n log n).

Describes the two-pointer method (one pointer at each end; move the left pointer up if the sum is too small, the right pointer down if it is too large), explains why it never skips a valid pair, and states it is O(n).

hintLadder: What's the simplest method you can think of, even if it's slow? How long does it take?
The array is sorted. For a given element a, what number are you looking for, and how quickly can you find it in a sorted array?
Try one pointer at the start and one at the end. If their sum is too small, which pointer should move?
When the sum is too large, the right element can't pair with anything between the pointers to make T. Why? Use that to argue no pair is missed.
probes: What changes if the array isn't sorted? Can you still beat O(n²)?
How would you count the number of pairs that sum to T, including duplicates?

misconceptions.signal: Allows an element to pair with itself, for example reports a[i] + a[i] = T as a valid pair.
misconceptions.realign: Quick check: the question asks for two different elements. Does your method ever pair an element with itself?

misconceptions.signal: In the two-pointer method, moves both pointers at once, moves the wrong pointer, or can't justify why no pair is skipped.
misconceptions.realign: Let's slow down on the pointers. If the current sum is too small, which single move can increase it, and why is it safe to discard that element?

problems.solutionSketch: Brute force checks all pairs, O(n²). Binary search for T − a[i] among the other elements gives O(n log n). Two pointers i = 0, j = n − 1: if a[i] + a[j] < T then i++, if it is greater than T then j--, otherwise found; stop when i ≥ j. When the sum is too small, a[i] is too small to pair with any remaining element, so discarding it is safe (symmetrically for too large). O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

problems.title: Odd handshakes
problems.statement: At a party, some pairs of people shake hands. Prove that the number of people who shook an odd number of hands is even.

checkpoints.description: Models the party as a graph: people are vertices, handshakes are edges, and each person's handshake count is their degree.
Shows the total of all handshake counts is twice the number of handshakes, because each handshake is counted once for each of its two people, so the total is even.
Concludes by parity: the people with even counts contribute an even amount, so the odd counts must sum to an even number, which requires an even number of odd-count people.

hintLadder: Can you draw the party as a diagram? What would the people and the handshakes be?
Add up everyone's handshake count. How does that total relate to the number of handshakes?
So the total is even. Split the people into those with even counts and those with odd counts. What can you say about each group's sum?
A sum of odd numbers is even exactly when there is an even number of them. Can you finish the argument?
probes: Is it possible for exactly one person to have shaken an odd number of hands? Why not?
Can everyone at a party of 5 shake exactly 3 hands? Justify your answer.

misconceptions.signal: Assumes every pair shakes hands (or some specific pattern) instead of an arbitrary set of handshakes.
misconceptions.realign: Careful: the question says some pairs shake hands, not all of them. Your argument needs to work for any set of handshakes.

misconceptions.signal: Argues that because the total is even, each person's count is even, or asserts the odd-count people number must be even without justification.
misconceptions.realign: The total being even doesn't make each count even. What do you actually know about a sum that includes some odd numbers?

problems.solutionSketch: Model as a graph. The sum of degrees counts each edge twice, so it equals 2E and is even. Even-degree vertices contribute an even total, so the degrees of the odd-degree vertices sum to an even number. A sum of k odd numbers has the same parity as k, so k is even.

problems.title: Finding the heavy coin
problems.statement: You have 9 identical-looking coins; one is slightly heavier. Using a balance scale, what is the smallest number of weighings that always finds the heavy coin? Then generalise to n coins.
problems.canvasHint: Sketch your weighing plan on the canvas.

checkpoints.description: Finds a 2-weighing strategy: split the coins 3–3–3, weigh two groups, then weigh two coins from the group that must contain the heavy coin.
Explains why 1 weighing can't work: a weighing has only 3 outcomes (left heavier, right heavier, balance), which can't distinguish 9 possibilities.
Generalises to the smallest k with 3^k ≥ n, i.e. ⌈log₃ n⌉ weighings, using the same three-way split together with the counting argument.

hintLadder: How many different results can a single weighing give you?
If each weighing can rule out two-thirds of the candidates, how should you split the 9 coins?
Weigh 3 against 3. Whatever happens, how many candidates are left, and how do you finish in one more weighing?
After k weighings you can tell apart at most 3^k cases. What does that say about the number of weighings needed for n coins?
probes: What if you don't know whether the odd coin is heavier or lighter? How many coins can you handle with 3 weighings?
Does your formula still work when n isn't a power of 3, say n = 10?

misconceptions.signal: Splits the coins into two halves each time, getting about log₂ n weighings (for example 3 or 4 for 9 coins), missing that leaving a group off the scale gives information.
misconceptions.realign: Halving works, but is it the best you can do? When you weigh, what does it tell you if the scale balances?

misconceptions.signal: Treats a weighing as a two-way result, ignoring that a balance also gives information, so the lower-bound argument uses 2^k.
misconceptions.realign: You've counted two possible results of a weighing. Is there a third? What does it mean when the scale balances?

problems.solutionSketch: Weigh 3 against 3: the heavier side, or the unweighed 3 if the scale balances, contains the coin. Then weigh 1 against 1 among those 3. That is 2 weighings. One weighing has only 3 outcomes, fewer than 9 cases, so 2 is optimal. In general k weighings distinguish at most 3^k cases, so the minimum is ⌈log₃ n⌉, achieved by splitting into three near-equal groups each time.

levels.descriptor: Doesn't find a way in, even with hints.
Finds a way in only after substantial hints.
Finds a sensible approach with occasional nudges.
Independently finds a clear approach and adapts it when needed.
Key steps are wrong or missing.
Mostly correct but with unjustified or incorrect steps.
Correct, with minor gaps in justification.
Correct and fully justified at every step.
Rarely explains thinking; hard to follow.
Explains some steps but leaves big gaps.
Explains reasoning clearly throughout, including doubts and dead ends.
Uses hints only when they're very explicit.
Uses hints well after a short delay.
Picks up subtle hints immediately and builds on them.

fallbackPrompt: Talk me through what you're thinking right now. What would you try next?
